headline: Mountains are Earth's wrinkles—pushed up over millions of years by colliding plates
universal_truth: The greatest heights are often built through pressure and collision
fun_facts: The Himalayas are still rising—about 5 millimeters per year as India pushes into Asia
Mount Everest contains marine fossils at its peak—it was once an ocean floor
Some mountains are older than trees; the Appalachians predate dinosaurs
discussion_questions: What pressures in your life have built you up rather than worn you down?
How does knowing Everest was once an ocean floor change how you see it?
What mountains are you building through persistent pressure?

hook.script: Stand at the base of a mountain and you're looking at millions of years of pressure made visible. Mountains are Earth's memory of collisions—continent slamming into continent, sea floor thrust skyward. They're monuments to the power of time and force.

cliff.script: The Himalayas contain fossils of sea creatures at 29,000 feet. How did an ancient ocean floor end up at the roof of the world? What force could lift seabed to sky?

options.text: Tectonic plates collide, and the crust crumples and folds upward
options.response: Yes. When continents collide, the crust buckles and rises over millions of years.

options.text: Volcanic activity builds mountains from erupted material
options.response: Volcanoes do build some mountains, but the tallest are formed differently...

fact1.title: Continental Collision
fact1.script: About 50 million years ago, India crashed into Asia and kept pushing. The crust crumpled like a rug pushed against a wall. The Himalayas rose—and continue rising today, 5 millimeters per year. Mountains are slow-motion collisions.

fact2.title: Seabed to Summit
fact2.script: Before collision, the ocean floor between India and Asia collected shells, corals, and sea creatures that became limestone. When the continents collided, this seafloor was thrust skyward. Everest's peak is made of ancient ocean.

fact3.title: Ancient Mountains
fact3.script: The Appalachian Mountains are 480 million years old—they predate dinosaurs, trees, and most land life. Once as tall as the Himalayas, erosion has worn them to gentle slopes. Every mountain is temporary; time is patient.

wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: The greatest heights come from pressure and collision. Mountains teach us that obstacles can lift us higher, that resistance builds structure, and that what seems like destruction can create majesty.

outro.script: That's Day 54. Tomorrow, we'll dive into the deep ocean mystery. Until then, if you see a mountain, see millions of years of pressure transformed into beauty.

growTrack.title: Pressure to Height - Reframe Your Challenges
growTrack.learning_objective: See challenges as potential mountain-building forces
growTrack.activity: Think of a major challenge or 'collision' in your past. How did it build you? What height did you gain from that pressure? Now apply this lens to a current challenge: how might this be building your mountain?
